C005.subject: Prolonged screen time from personal digital devices in high-income countries
C005.object: self-reported life satisfaction among adolescents, controlling for income, only when screen time is predominantly passive (e.g., scrolling, watching) rather than interactive
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Prolonged screen time from personal digital devices in high-income countries self-reported life satisfaction among adolescents, controlling for income, only when screen time is predominantly passive (e.g., scrolling, watching) rather than interactive]

[PATH:empirical] Large-scale panel study (e.g., Millennium Cohort Study or German Socio-Economic Panel) that separately measures passive vs. interactive screen time in adolescents, alongside repeated measures of life satisfaction, with fixed-effects models controlling for income and prior well-being. — A longitudinal design with within-person comparisons can disentangle temporal ordering and reduce reverse causation. Distinguishing passive from interactive use tests the key moderator, and controlling for income addresses the specified scope. This would directly confirm or refute the causal claim.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental micro-study: Randomly assign adolescents to 30–60 minutes of either passive scrolling (e.g., TikTok feed) or interactive engagement (e.g., collaborative game or creative app), then measure immediate and delayed self-reported life satisfaction and affect, with baseline control. — Experimental manipulation provides the strongest causal evidence. Comparing passive vs. interactive conditions isolates the moderating role of engagement type. Short-term effects can be extrapolated to prolonged exposure patterns hypothesized in C005.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of existing literature on screen time and adolescent well-being, meta-analyzing studies that differentiate passive vs. active use, and assessing effect size heterogeneity with income as a covariate. — Synthesizing available evidence from multiple studies can reveal whether the passive/interactive distinction consistently moderates the effect, and whether income controls are sufficient. This provides theoretical coherence and identifies gaps in current evidence.

qualifier.note: Distinguishes between passive and active screen use as a key moderating variable, potentially resolving some reverse causation concerns by testing whether the type of engagement matters for the directional effect.

C006.subject: Increased social media use among adolescents in high-income countries
C006.object: higher self-reported life satisfaction, when online interactions strengthen real-world friendships
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Increased social media use among adolescents in high-income countries higher self-reported life satisfaction, when online interactions strengthen real-world friendships]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel study measuring social media use, friendship quality, and life satisfaction in adolescents (e.g., using data from the UK Millennium Cohort Study or the German Socio-Economic Panel) — Such a study can track within-individual changes over time to test whether increases in social media use that strengthen real-world friendships precede improvements in life satisfaction, while controlling for baseline well-being and confounding variables.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental design that manipulates the nature of online interactions (e.g., encouraging supportive vs. passive social media use) among adolescent friend groups — Directly testing the causal role of friendship-strengthening interactions by randomly assigning participants to conditions that foster online social support versus passive consumption, then measuring subsequent life satisfaction.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing studies on social media, friendship quality, and adolescent well-being, with a focus on moderator analyses for friendship reinforcement — Synthesizing available evidence can clarify whether the hypothesized positive correlation holds consistently across different measurement methods and populations, and identify gaps in the current literature.

qualifier.note: If screen time facilitates social connection and support, the correlation reverses or disappears, disproving a simple negative relationship.

C007.subject: Productivity-enhancing technology adoption in high-income workplaces
C007.object: work intensification and monitoring pressures, eroding autonomy gains and worsening well-being compared to low-income workplaces
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Productivity-enhancing technology adoption in high-income workplaces work intensification and monitoring pressures, eroding autonomy gains and worsening well-being compared to low-income workplaces]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies comparing autonomy and well-being metrics (e.g., job strain, work pace) across high-income vs. low-income workplaces after adoption of productivity-enhancing technologies (e.g., AI, monitoring software). Data sources: UK Understanding Society, German SOEP, US General Social Survey (2010-2023). — Directly tests whether high-income workplaces experience greater erosion of autonomy and declines in well-being relative to low-income counterparts, using repeated measures to capture temporal dynamics.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies on employee monitoring technology (e.g., time-tracking, surveillance software) and its effects on perceived autonomy, stress, and job satisfaction, stratified by occupational income level. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether work intensification and monitoring pressures are systematically stronger in high-income settings, potentially refuting the hypothesis if no differential effect is found.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative ethnographic case studies of technology adoption in high-income (e.g., tech firms, finance) and low-income (e.g., retail, manufacturing) work settings, examining changes in workplace autonomy, monitoring, and worker well-being. — Provides qualitative depth to understand mechanisms (e.g., how technology reshapes control and discretion) and contextual factors that might moderate the hypothesized relationship, helping confirm or elaborate the claim.

qualifier.geographic: United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and South Korea

C008.subject: Productivity-enhancing technology adoption in high-income workplaces
C008.object: work flexibility and autonomy, intensifying well-being declines from surveillance and algorithmic management
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Productivity-enhancing technology adoption in high-income workplaces work flexibility and autonomy, intensifying well-being declines from surveillance and algorithmic management]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel surveys of knowledge workers in North America and Western Europe (e.g., European Working Conditions Survey, American Working Conditions Survey) measuring changes in perceived autonomy, trust, and well-being coincident with firm-level adoption of productivity-enhancing technologies like remote monitoring software. — This source can directly test the temporal relationship claimed in the hypothesis by comparing pre- and post-technology adoption well-being and autonomy measures, controlling for confounders such as industry and job role.

[PATH:literature] Qualitative case studies or meta-analyses in organizational sociology and management journals (e.g., Administrative Science Quarterly, Journal of Organizational Behavior) examining the effects of algorithmic management and surveillance on employee discretion and flexibility in high-income tech firms. — A systematic literature review can synthesize existing findings to assess the consistency of the hypothesis across different contexts, identifying moderating factors like managerial culture or technology design that might strengthen or weaken the claimed relationship.

[PATH:empirical] Field experiments or quasi-experimental studies in workplaces adopting new productivity tools (e.g., time-tracking software, AI-driven scheduling) with randomized rollout or matched comparison groups, measuring well-being, perceived autonomy, and turnover intentions. — Causal evidence from controlled or quasi-controlled settings can help disentangle the net effect of technology adoption from pre-existing trends, providing stronger confirmation or refutation of the hypothesis than correlational data alone.

qualifier.geographic: high-income countries, primarily North America and Western Europe

C011.subject: Long-term technology adoption in high-income countries
C011.predicate: reduces aggregate subjective well-being only when
C011.object: the technology primarily facilitates conspicuous consumption and status signaling, rather than time-saving or leisure-enhancing uses
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Long-term technology adoption in high-income countries the technology primarily facilitates conspicuous consumption and status signaling, rather than time-saving or leisure-enhancing uses]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from high-income countries (e.g., World Values Survey, Eurobarometer) on technology adoption categories (status signaling vs. leisure/time-saving) linked to subjective well-being measures, analyzing within-country variation over time. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing well-being trends for different technology domains, controlling for confounds like income and social norms.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on status consumption and well-being (e.g., randomly assigned peer comparison feedback in technology purchase contexts). — Provides causal evidence on whether conspicuous technology adoption reduces well-being, distinguishing it from other consumption motives.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of status signaling and hedonic adaptation (e.g., Frank's positionality theory, Kahneman's focusing illusion), applied to technology adoption. — Offers a mechanistic framework predicting that status-signaling technologies trigger relative deprivation and adaptation, whereas time-saving/leisure technologies improve well-being through increased free time or enjoyment.

qualifier.note: Predicts that the negative well-being effect is contingent on the consumption domain in which technology is adopted, with leisure-oriented technology adoption producing null or positive effects.

C012.subject: Long-term technology adoption in high-income countries
C012.object: rising income inequality and social comparison pressures, reducing aggregate subjective well-being
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Long-term technology adoption in high-income countries rising income inequality and social comparison pressures, reducing aggregate subjective well-being]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of the World Values Survey and European Social Survey (1990-2020) for high-income countries, measuring subjective well-being alongside income inequality (Gini coefficients) and internet/social media penetration rates as proxies for social comparison pressures. — Directly tests the temporal correlation between technology adoption, rising inequality, social comparison, and well-being at the aggregate level, controlling for other macroeconomic factors.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of experimental studies on social media use and subjective well-being (e.g., randomized control trials limiting Facebook/Instagram use), combined with macro-level data on technology diffusion and income distribution. — Synthesizes micro-level causal evidence on social comparison effects with macro-level trends, helping to assess whether the hypothesized pathway operates as claimed.

[PATH:theoretical] Counterfactual simulation using a calibrated macroeconomic agent-based model that tracks technology adoption, earnings distribution, and well-being under varying social comparison intensities and redistribution policies. — Tests the plausibility and sensitivity of the causal chain in a controlled environment, identifying conditions under which the hypothesis holds or fails.
